mainEntity.name: Can I keep taking ibuprofen until my dental appointment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Over-the-counter pain relief such as ibuprofen or paracetamol may help manage mild to moderate tooth discomfort in the short term whilst you wait for a dental appointment. However, it is important to follow the dosage instructions on the packaging and not exceed the recommended amount. Pain relief should be viewed as a temporary measure only — it does not address the underlying cause of tooth pain. If your pain is severe, increasing, or accompanied by swelling or fever, contact a dental practice or NHS 111 promptly rather than waiting.

mainEntity.name: Why does my toothache feel worse at night?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many people notice that tooth pain intensifies at night or when lying down. This is partly because blood pressure in the head increases when you are horizontal, which can heighten the sensation of throbbing or pulsing pain. Additionally, there are fewer distractions at night, which may make pain feel more prominent. Persistent nocturnal toothache is one of the signs that dental assessment may be warranted sooner rather than later.

mainEntity.name: Is a tooth abscess dangerous if left untreated?

acceptedAnswer.text: A dental abscess is a bacterial infection and, like any infection, has the potential to progress if it is not treated. In most cases, prompt dental treatment effectively resolves the infection. In rare circumstances, untreated dental infections can spread to surrounding tissues or, in very serious cases, beyond the jaw. For this reason, any suspected dental abscess — particularly if accompanied by facial swelling, fever, or difficulty swallowing — should be assessed by a dental professional without delay. This article is educational in nature and does not constitute a clinical diagnosis.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a reversible and irreversible toothache?

acceptedAnswer.text: Broadly speaking, reversible dental pain is pain that resolves once the source of irritation is removed — for example, brief sensitivity when eating cold food that disappears quickly. Irreversible pain tends to linger, occur spontaneously, or worsen over time, suggesting that the nerve tissue inside the tooth may be significantly affected. The distinction between these categories requires clinical assessment and cannot reliably be determined from symptoms alone, which is why a dental examination is always the appropriate next step for persistent or unexplained tooth pain.

mainEntity.name: Should I go to A&E for tooth pain?

acceptedAnswer.text: In most cases, a dental practice — either your regular dentist or an emergency dental service — is the most appropriate place to seek help for tooth pain. Accident and emergency departments in hospitals are not typically equipped to provide definitive dental treatment. However, if you experience severe swelling that is affecting your ability to breathe or swallow, high fever alongside dental pain, or significant swelling spreading to your neck or eye area, seeking urgent medical attention at A&E is appropriate. NHS 111 can also provide guidance on the most suitable next steps if you are uncertain.

mainEntity.name: How quickly can a dental infection become serious?

acceptedAnswer.text: The rate at which a dental infection progresses varies considerably between individuals and depends on factors including general health, immune function, and the nature of the infection. Some infections remain localised for an extended period, whilst others can progress more rapidly. Because it is not possible to predict the course of any individual infection without clinical assessment, dental infections should generally be evaluated by a dental professional as soon as practically possible rather than managed with pain relief alone and monitored at home indefinitely.
